newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq still conceals data on its weapons - Ekeus.
newsitem.headline: Iraq still conceals data on its weapons - Ekeus.

text.p: Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus said on Monday that Iraq had not given any new information about unaccounted weapons but added the two agreed to focus on this issue.
"We have not cleared up any more issues," said Ekeus at the end of three-day visit to Baghdad during which he met senior Iraqi officials including Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz.
But Ekeus added: "We have discussed approaches (to resolve the issue of missing arms)...We have agreed to focus on this issue."
He refused to go into details.

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of ridding Baghdad of mass destruction weapons -- headed by Ekeus -- has said that Iraq was still hiding small but highly significant quantities of banned arms.
"We feel and convinced that we have not accounted for all prohibited weapons (in Iraq)," he said.

A clean bill of health by the commission is a key requirement by the U.N. Security Council before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under crippling trade sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
"We cannot verify that Iraq does not possess weapons or components...We have information and data which contradict that for the moment," Ekeus said.
Iraqi media and officials have been lashing out at the UNSCOM, saying that it was influenced by anti-Iraq policies of the United States and Britain.
The government newspaper al-Qadissiya condemned the commission on Monday, saying that some of its inspectors were recruited by the U.S. Central Intellegence Agency.
Ekeus said the missing weapons were in the three main areas of ballistic, chemical and biological.
Concerning ballistic missiles, he said the commission had "neutralised (Iraq's) programmes" but had not accounted for "hopefully not more than 16" missiles.
"We counted, counted and counted but we have not (yet) accounted for all missiles," he said.
He said that concerning chemical weapons, the inspectors still wanted to know more about certain production.
Ekeus said that he still needed to clear up Iraq's declaration that it only had acquired small amount of biological weapons.
Ekeus said his commission was successful in destroying Iraq's main biological weapons production factory, al-Hakam.
He said that he would visit Iraq in December to continue dialogue with the Iraqi government on its past weapons programmes.
